description_ru: Юмористический рассказ о закваске по имени Джеральд, которая росла, как живое существо, и превратила автора в пекаря.
text:
It all started with a jar of flour and water. My neighbour Doris, who is eighty years old and makes the best bread in our street, gave me a small spoonful of sticky grey mixture and called it a sourdough starter. "Feed it every day," she told me, "and it will live for ever." I thanked her politely, took it home, and put it in a jar on my kitchen counter. I did not know that I was bringing a new family member into my house.

At first the starter was easy to look after. I fed it a little flour and water every morning, and I watched it make small bubbles, like a very slow fizzy drink. After three days it smelled slightly sour, a bit like old socks, and my wife said that she was not sure about it. I explained that this was normal. "It is alive," I said proudly. "It is a living thing." She looked at the jar for a long time and replied, "I know. That is what worries me."

The next week I decided to give it a name, because everybody seemed to do this. The internet was full of people who had called their starters things like Doughy Parton and Bread Pitt, and I thought that I should join them. After some thought, I named mine Gerald. Gerald was a calm, slow and rather smelly gentleman, and I felt that he suited the name. I talked to him every morning while I fed him. My wife thought that this was strange, but she did not stop me, which is what marriage is about.

I soon discovered that Gerald had a great appetite. When I forgot to feed him for two days, he grew so much that he pushed the lid off the jar and crept down the side onto the counter. I found him in the morning like a pale, bubbling monster, and I had to clean the entire kitchen. If I had known that starters could do this, I would have bought a bigger jar. That afternoon I bought three, plus a book called "The Sourdough Handbook", which I read in a single night.

My first loaf was a disaster. I followed the instructions carefully, but the dough would not rise, and when I finally took it out of the oven, it looked like a hockey puck. My wife tried to eat a slice and said that it tasted "very honest". I tapped it with a spoon, and it made a noise like a stone. Doris told me that I had not waited long enough and that real bread needs patience. "You cannot hurry a loaf," she said, giving me a second spoonful of starter, just in case.

The second loaf was better, and the third was almost good. By the end of the month, I could make a decent round loaf with a golden crust and a soft inside, and I was proud. I put a photograph of it on the internet, and I received eleven likes, mostly from members of my family. Encouraged, I started to bake every weekend. I experimented with seeds, olives and even chocolate, and for a while the whole house smelled wonderful. I also produced a lot of bread. By March, our freezer was full, and we had begun giving loaves to the postman, the neighbours and the people at my wife's office.

The trouble began when Gerald grew too successful. Because I was baking so often, I had to feed him twice a day, and I could not go on holiday without finding someone to look after him. For our anniversary, my wife booked a weekend in the mountains. I spent the whole journey worrying, and I called my sister every three hours to ask whether Gerald was still alive. She told me that he was fine, but that he was "making a noise". When we returned home, the jar was in the middle of the table, and my sister had decorated it with a small ribbon.

I have now been baking for nearly a year, and Gerald and I have developed a strong friendship. I know that he likes warm rooms and dislikes cold ones, that he works hardest in the afternoon, and that he becomes very excited when I give him rye flour. Doris says that I am now an expert, and she has asked me to teach a class at the community centre. I am nervous, but I have also decided to bring Gerald to the class. If somebody asks him a difficult question, I know that he will give a good answer. He is, after all, the oldest member of the family.

focus_sounds.tip_ru: Кончик языка слегка между зубами, воздух проходит без голоса; не заменяйте на «с» или «ф».
Губы округлены и вытянуты вперёд, зубов не касаются; это не русское «в».
Спинка языка прижата к нёбу, звук идёт через нос; в конце -ing не добавляйте «г».
Ударный слог длиннее, громче и выше по тону; остальные слоги сокращаются, особенно в длинных словах.

questions.question: Who gave the narrator the sourdough starter?
What did the starter do when he forgot to feed it?
questions.answer: It grew, pushed the lid off the jar and crept onto the counter.

questions.question: What was the first loaf like?
questions.answer: It looked like a hockey puck and sounded like a stone.

questions.question: Why did the narrator worry on the anniversary weekend?
questions.answer: He called his sister every three hours to ask if Gerald was still alive.
